interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the turning arm's height, carried across and traced against time, drawing one whole sine wave for every turn when you set the arm turning steadily.
interactive.title: The arm and its wave
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in sixteen small screens, most on one picture, the arm and its wave. On the left is lesson 3's circle with its arm, turning anticlockwise at a steady speed from pointing right. A dashed line carries the tip's height across to a graph on the right, whose across axis is time and whose up axis is height, and a pen on that line draws the height as time goes on, so the wave grows from left to right. The rule is the one from Round the circle: an arm of length 1 has its tip at height sin θ, and an arm of length E at E sin θ. Because the arm turns steadily, its angle grows in step with time. Where the arm can be dragged, its tip wears a ring. On screens that show an idea, sliders set the arm's length, its turns a second (with its angular speed ω = 2π × turns a second beside it, in rad/s) and the angle it starts from; a pause button freezes it to read the height; a switch traces the arm's across shadow instead of its height. Screen 1 turns an arm of length 1 once: the trace rises to 1 at a quarter turn, is back at 0 at a half turn, falls to −1 at three quarters and returns to 0 at a full turn, one whole wave for one turn. Screen 2 freezes the arm at a half turn, pointing left, and asks where the trace is: 0, −1 (the across shadow read instead of the height) or 1. Screen 3 sets the arm's length to 10: the wave now runs between 10 and −10, and its peak is labelled amplitude, the stretch from Functions and their graphs. Screen 4 freezes an arm of length 4 at 30° and asks its height: 2 (4 × sin 30°), 3.46 (4 × cos 30°, the across shadow) or 0.5 (sin 30° with the length left out). Screen 5 turns the arm 2 times a second on a graph one second wide, and two whole waves fill it, each taking 0.5 s, marked as the period; sliding the turns a second from 1 to 10 packs that many waves into the same second, and a row works out a UK supply's period at 50 Hz, 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02 s, 20 ms. Screen 6 asks for the frequency of a wave that repeats every 10 ms: 100 Hz (1 ÷ 0.01), 0.01 (the period read as the frequency) or 10 (the milliseconds read as hertz). Screen 7 marks one turn as 2π radians round the circle, so the arm's angle after t seconds is ωt with ω = 2πf, and the label reads height = E sin(2πft); at 50 Hz the ω readout shows 314.16 rad/s, and at 60 Hz, common on ships, ω is 376.99 rad/s, a wave every 16.7 ms; written as 4 sin(2π × 5t), a wave can be read straight off, peak 4 at 5 Hz. Screen 8 asks for the frequency of v = 10 sin(100πt): 50 Hz (100π ÷ 2π), 314.2 (ω read as the frequency) or 100 (the 100 read off as the frequency, forgetting the 2 in 2π). Screen 9 sets the start angle of a second arm, B, anywhere from −180° to 180°: started a quarter turn on (π/2, 90°), it is already at the top at t = 0, and its wave is the first wave slid left by a quarter period, 5 ms at 50 Hz; started behind, at a negative angle, its wave slides right, later; the switch traces the first arm's across shadow, which draws exactly the π/2 wave, the cosine wave. Screen 10 shows wave A from an arm started pointing right and asks about wave B, from an arm started π/2 behind: B is A slid right by a quarter period, slid left by a quarter period, or twice as tall. Screen 11 draws a level line at 5 across the wave 10 sin(100πt): lying between the peaks, it meets each wave twice, as lesson 3's level line met the circle twice. The height is 5 when sin(100πt) = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5. In radian mode sin⁻¹ 0.5 = 0.524, and the other angle with the same sine is π − 0.524 = 2.618; the arm's angle is ωt, so each time is the angle ÷ ω, and the times are 0.524 ÷ 314.16 = 1.67 ms and 2.618 ÷ 314.16 = 8.33 ms. Screen 12 puts the line at −8.3 and asks when the wave first reaches it: 13.1 ms (sin⁻¹(−0.83) = −0.979, so the arm is there at π + 0.979 = 4.121 radians, ÷ 314.16), 3.1 ms (the minus sign dropped, 0.979 ÷ 314.16, when the wave is at +8.3, not −8.3) or 16.9 ms (the second crossing, 2π − 0.979 = 5.304 radians). Screen 13 swaps the height for the arm's slope, tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ from Round the circle, traced against the angle: 0 at 0°, 1 at 45°, climbing without limit as the arm nears straight up, so the graph is cut off at 4 and −4 with small arrows, with no value at 90° and 270°, where the across shadow is 0. It repeats every half turn, because an arm half a turn on points the opposite way, both its shadows change sign, and their ratio is the same. Screen 14 freezes the arm at 135°, up and to the left, and asks whether tan 135° is positive, negative or has no value: negative, since sin 135° = 0.707 and cos 135° = −0.707 give −1; positive drops the minus of the across shadow, and no value belongs only to 90° and 270°. Screens 15 and 16 are mixed. A supply peaks at 325 V at 50 Hz: is its wave 325 sin(314.2t), 325 sin(50t) (the frequency used as ω) or 325 sin(100t) (the π left out)? A wave is v = 20 sin(ωt + π/2): at t = 0, is v 20 (the arm starts straight up), 0 (the phase left out) or 1 (sin π/2, the length left out)? Each puzzle offers three answers; a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? draws the answer on the picture.
interactive.ignores: The arm turns at a perfectly steady speed, so the wave is a perfect sine; a real supply's wave is close to this shape but not exactly it. The pen draws far slower than a real 50 Hz supply, which makes fifty waves every second. The arm is drawn at its peak length; many electrical texts draw the arrow at the rms value instead, the same shape made smaller, which Adding waves with phasors takes up. Readouts are rounded while the working keeps every figure, and the lengths, voltages and the 10 ms period are example figures.

explain.text:
Set lesson 3's arm turning at a steady speed, carry its tip's height across to a graph of height against time, and the trace is a sine wave, the shape of an AC supply's voltage: the arm's length sets how tall it is, its turns a second set how many waves fit in a second, and the angle it starts from sets where the wave starts.

Remember Round the circle: an arm of length 1 has its tip at (cos θ, sin θ), so its height is sin θ.[^2] An arm of length E is the same picture drawn E times bigger, so its tip's height is E sin θ. Turning at a steady speed means the angle grows by the same amount every second, so equal steps of time are equal steps of angle, and the height plotted against time takes the same shape as sin θ plotted against the angle: up to E at a quarter turn, back to 0 at a half turn, down to −E at three quarters, and 0 again at a full turn, where it starts over. So a sine wave can be thought of as the height of an arrow turning at a constant speed, like a clock's second hand, though the other way round, whose length is the wave's height, its [[amplitude]].[^3] An arm E long stretches the wave of sin θ upwards by E, the stretch you met in Functions and their graphs. For an AC voltage, the up part of the turning arrow gives the voltage at each instant.[^4]

One turn draws one whole wave, so the turns a second are the waves a second: the [[frequency]], the number of cycles in one second,[^5] counted in hertz. UK low-voltage supplies are declared at 50 hertz unless otherwise agreed in writing,[^1] so each wave takes 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02 seconds, 20 ms, a time called the period. Radians count the same turning in radius-lengths: one turn, 360°, is 2π radians,[^6] so f turns a second is 2πf radians a second, the arm's angular speed ω. After t seconds the arm has turned ωt radians from pointing right, so its height is E sin(ωt) = E sin(2πft).[^7] At 50 Hz, ω = 2π × 50 = 314.16 rad/s. Ships often run at 60 Hz instead, which a college's notes on marine electrical systems call the most common frequency on board ship;[^8] there ω = 2π × 60 = 376.99 rad/s, and a wave takes 1 ÷ 60 s, 16.7 ms. Because ωt is in radians, the calculator goes in radian mode.

If the arm starts at an angle φ instead of pointing right, it has a head start: after t seconds it is at ωt + φ, so the wave is E sin(ωt + φ). Turning at ω radians a second, the first arm needs φ ÷ ω seconds to turn through φ, so the second arm reaches every height φ ÷ ω seconds sooner, and the whole wave slides that far left, the shift you met in Functions and their graphs; the starting angle is the wave's [[phase]]. An arm started behind, at a negative φ, reaches every height later, and its wave slides right. Start the arm a quarter turn on, at π/2. It is then always the first arm turned a further quarter turn anticlockwise, and a quarter turn anticlockwise carries whatever lay along the across axis up onto the up axis, so this arm's height is always the first arm's across shadow: E sin(ωt + π/2) = E cos ωt. The cosine wave is the sine wave started a quarter turn early. **A steadily turning arm's height against time is the sine wave E sin(2πft): E is the arm's length, f its turns a second, and 2πf its angular speed ω in radians a second.[^7]**

analogy.text: Watch a cyclist from the side, pedalling steadily. The pedal goes round a circle, but its height alone rises and falls: highest at the top, level with the axle at the front and at the back, lowest at the bottom. Plot that height against time and you have the sine wave: a longer crank draws a taller wave, faster pedalling fits more waves into each second, and where the pedal was when you started the clock sets the phase.
analogy.breaks: Real pedalling is not perfectly steady: riders push harder on the way down, so the pedal speeds up and slows a little and its height traces a wave that is close to a sine but not exactly one. The height is measured from the axle, not from the road.

practice.text:
- Read a wave written E sin(2πft) or E sin(ωt): E is the peak, the arm's length; f is turns a second, in hertz; ω = 2πf is radians a second. So 4 sin(2π × 5t) peaks at 4 and turns 5 times a second, 5 Hz.
- From ω to f, divide by 2π. From f to the period, work out 1 ÷ f.
- Put the calculator in radian mode: ωt is in radians.
- A + φ inside the bracket means the arm started φ further round, so the wave is slid left, earlier; a − φ means it started φ behind, so the wave is slid right, later.
- To find when the wave reaches a height h: work out h ÷ E, take sin⁻¹ in radian mode, find the second angle with the same sine (π minus the first), bring both into 0 to 2π, then divide each by ω.

**Rule of thumb:** At 50 Hz one wave takes 20 ms, and ω is about 314 rad/s, which is 100π. At 60 Hz, common on ships,[^8] one wave takes 16.7 ms and ω is 376.99 rad/s.

**Worked example:** UK low-voltage supplies are declared at 230 V between phase and neutral and 50 Hz, unless otherwise agreed in writing.[^1] UK mains voltages are quoted as r.m.s. values,[^9] the peak ÷ √2 from Calculus fundamentals, so the peak is 230 × √2 = 325.3 V. With ω = 2π × 50 = 314.16 rad/s, the supply is v = 325.3 sin(314.16t). At t = 2.5 ms the arm has turned 314.16 × 0.0025 = 0.785 radians, an eighth of a turn, and v = 325.3 × sin 0.785 = 230.0 V.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading the across shadow as the height: the sine is the height, the cosine the across.
- Using f where ω belongs: 325 sin(50t) turns 50 radians a second, 7.96 turns, not 50.
- Reading the period as the frequency: a wave that repeats every 10 ms has a frequency of 1 ÷ 0.01 = 100 Hz.
- Degrees mode on sin(314.16t): the calculator then reads 0.785 as degrees.
- Taking only the calculator's one angle: a level line between the peaks meets each wave twice.
